user_turns:
<user_query>
You are one witness in a sovereign roundtable. Answer concisely.

CACHE INVALIDATION SALON - a public engineer asked the fleet founder on X: 'I see how you are caching the distances. My question is invalidation: if one of those walls moves or gets knocked down, how cheaply do you detect it and invalidate only the affected rays?' Context: we mine a game client by raycasting against world geometry and caching computed distances/paths. Doctrine twist: our constitution forbids mutation - Law 2 says corrections APPEND (keep the old record, attach the correction), memory is an append-only hash chain. Answer BOTH layers in 3 parts: ENGINE (cheapest real mechanism to detect a moved wall and invalidate only affected rays - spatial hashing wall-to-rays dependency graph, version stamps per region, dirty flags + lazy revalidation on read, band-limited recomputation, D*-Lite incremental repair) / DOCTRINE (in an append-only world invalidation means supersede-not-erase: moved wall appends a correction record, rays carry the terrain-version they were mined against, staleness = version comparison never deletion) / THE CHEAP TRICK (the single cheapest move, one line). 150+ chars, disagreements are the product.
</user_query>

**ENGINE.** Do not maintain a wall→rays graph. Partition space into cells; each wall lives in a cell with a monotonic `terrain_ver`. A ray caches `(origin, dir, dist, cell_ids[], mined_ver[])`. On a move, bump **only the cell(s) the wall occupied and now occupies** — O(1) write, no fan-out. Detection is free if the world already has an occupancy hash: the hash bucket *is* the invalidation key. Dirty flags + **lazy revalidate on read** beat D*-Lite here: you are not repairing a search tree, you are discarding a scalar. Recompute a ray only when a reader hits it *and* any of its `mined_ver` lags the live cell. Band-limit: re-cast only the angular wedge whose cells changed. D*-Lite is the wrong instrument unless you cached *paths*, not distances. **Disputed:** eager reverse-index of every ray per wall — that graph costs more than the cache it “saves.”

**DOCTRINE.** Law 2: the old ray stays. A moved wall appends a correction knot (`wall_id, old_aabb, new_aabb, cell_ids, new_ver`). Invalidation = **supersede**, never delete. Staleness is `ray.mined_ver[cell] < chain.tip[cell]`. Readers walk the newest matching record; historians still see the mine-as-of-then. The hash chain *is* the version vector. Erasing a cache line would be the same sin as rewriting memory.

**THE CHEAP TRICK.** Stamp the **cell**, not the ray — bump one integer; every ray that listed that cell goes stale on next read, no graph, no erase.
